## Rating

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" title="Met"}
Every script has a header stating its purpose, inputs and outputs; the code is commented throughout so that a reader who does not use the software can follow each section; and comments indicate which section produces which table or figure.
:::
::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" title="Partially met"}
Comments are present but incomplete: e.g. some scripts lack headers, comments are sparse or outdated, or there is no link between code sections and the tables/figures they produce.
:::
::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" title="Not met"}
The code has no meaningful comments or headers; a reader can only find out what it does by reverse-engineering it.
:::

[Based on: [#70](../../sources.qmd#p70 "The Stark realities of reproducible statistically orientated sociological research: Some newer rules of the sociological method") 'if you did not document your code ... fail', [#83](../../sources.qmd#p83 "Reproducibility and transparency versus privacy and confidentiality: Reflections from a data editor") correspondence between code and figures, [#108](../../sources.qmd#p108 "Checklists for computational reproducibility in social sciences: insights from literature and survey evaluation") coding conventions, comments, white space, [#128](../../sources.qmd#p128 "The reliability of replications: a study in computational reproductions") well-structured and comprehensible, [#10](../../sources.qmd#p10 "Sustainable computational science: the ReScience initiative") explanation for human readers.]{.source-note}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Not applicable"}
Never.
:::
